articles.title: Your Gumroad product is published and still invisible — the 10 conditions nobody reads
articles.excerpt: I ran a measurement this week that I expected to be boring and turned out to explain four weeks of zero. A store with five published products. I searched Gumroad's own Discover for six phrases a buyer…
articles.body: I ran a measurement this week that I expected to be boring and turned out to explain four weeks of zero. A store with five published products. I searched Gumroad's own Discover for six phrases a buyer would plausibly type — "landing page audit", "website audit", "landing page checklist", "conversion audit", "landing page review", "website review". Each query returned 36 products . The store appeared in none of them . Then I searched for the store's own product names. Then for the store's own username. Still nothing — while comparable third-party products showed up in the same result sets, with prices from $0 to $497. That is not a ranking problem. That is an inclusion problem, and Gumroad documents it.

articles.title: Your agent passed 10,000 evals. It can still deadlock.
articles.excerpt: If your agent workflow has 20 routing variables — retry counters, confidence thresholds, tool-success flags, budget checks — the guards on its edges combine in 2^20 = 1,048,576 ways. Run 10,000 evals…
articles.body: If your agent workflow has 20 routing variables — retry counters, confidence thresholds, tool-success flags, budget checks — the guards on its edges combine in 2^20 = 1,048,576 ways. Run 10,000 evals and you have sampled under 1% of them (0.95%, to be exact). The other 99% is where the stalls live. A green eval suite proves the workflow can work. It says nothing about the combinations you didn't sample — including the ones where every outgoing edge of some node is closed at the same time and the agent has nowhere to go. The failure mode This is an illustrative example, but the shape is common. Take a research agent with a critic loop: a planner calls a tool executor, a critic node checks the result, and two edges leave the critic.
articles.author: IdeaSniper

articles.title: How I Fixed TTS Hallucinations Without Regenerating Everything
articles.excerpt: The audit had done its job. I knew where the generated audiobook didn’t match the manuscript. Now I had another problem. Most of the audio around those errors was already good. The pacing worked. The…
articles.body: The audit had done its job. I knew where the generated audiobook didn’t match the manuscript. Now I had another problem. Most of the audio around those errors was already good. The pacing worked. The voices worked. The performances worked. Regenerating an entire chapter to fix one localized problem meant asking the TTS model to recreate all of that again. And generative audio isn’t deterministic in the ways that matter here. A new generation could change the pacing, emphasis, pauses, emotional delivery, or interaction between voices. I might fix one sentence and lose a performance I already liked. So I stopped thinking about the chapter as something that needed to be regenerated. I started treating it like recorded audio that needed a punch-in.
articles.author: Julian Brown

articles.title: Building a Client-Side QR Code Debugger with 6 Optical Tests and 10 Languages
articles.excerpt: Have you ever scanned a QR code that looked perfectly fine on a high-resolution screen, but failed miserably when printed? It happens all the time. Low contrast, missing quiet zones, or oversized logo…
articles.body: Have you ever scanned a QR code that looked perfectly fine on a high-resolution screen, but failed miserably when printed? It happens all the time. Low contrast, missing quiet zones, or oversized logos can easily break the error correction data inside a QR code, rendering it useless to smartphone cameras. To solve this, we built the RahaLune QR Code Debugger. It is a 100% client-side tool that runs six standardized optical tests on any uploaded QR code image, giving users a clear scannability score before they send anything to the printer. Recently, we rolled out a massive update: native translation into 10 languages, including full Right-to-Left layout support for Arabic and Urdu. Here is a look at how we built it and the technical challenges we solved along the way.

articles.title: The 73-Second Hallucination: Building Automated QA for Generative TTS
articles.excerpt: In my previous article, I wrote about solving ear fatigue in long-form TTS: repeated cadence, unnatural pacing, and the tendency for generated narration to fall into predictable patterns. One of the c…
articles.body: In my previous article, I wrote about solving ear fatigue in long-form TTS: repeated cadence, unnatural pacing, and the tendency for generated narration to fall into predictable patterns. One of the conclusions I came away with was that higher temperature gave the model more room to vary its performance without changing the words. Then I listened to the final master of Chapter 9. At 03:48 , the script called for a short exchange: Sarah: “You made dinner?” Daniel: “I tried.” Instead, the model kept going. It invented new dialogue. Then more dialogue. Then blocking, reactions, and tension that weren’t anywhere in the manuscript. For roughly 73 seconds, it wrote and performed its own version of the story.

articles.title: Black holes can split in two — but only if they spin at extreme speeds
articles.excerpt: Scientists have long known that when two black holes collide, they merge to create a more massive black hole. New research suggests that the opposite may happen too: single black holes may split in tw…
articles.body: Scientists have long known that when two black holes collide, they merge to create a more massive black hole. These events are so violent that they set the very fabric of space ringing with ripples called gravitational waves. Now, new research suggests that the opposite may happen, too: single black holes may be able to split in two. But this can only happen if that progenitor black hole is spinning at maximum possible speed. That speed prevents the black holes from immediately falling back on each other. There are physical laws in place that would usually prevent black holes from splitting in two; the team behind this research investigated whether there are conditions in which these laws can be temporarily bypassed.
articles.author: Robert Lea

articles.title: How 'spacewalking' underwater made me feel like I was really in space
articles.excerpt: Analog Astronaut Commander and Aquanaut Michaela Musilova led underwater simulated “spacewalks” in low visibility to test astronaut safety and communication protocols during simulated space missions.
articles.body: I was breathing just fine through my life support systems, but I kept feeling an urge to double check that everything was ok with my "spacesuit" before heading out on this "spacewalk." I have worn many different types of spacesuits on Earth during my career, but for the first time in my life, I knew that I couldn’t just stop to breathe the air outside if there were an emergency. That's because I was underwater. On this excursion, I was leading a simulated space mission underwater called SEA STAR. My " spacesuit " was actually scuba diving gear, and the simulated spacewalks , or EVAs (Extra-Vehicular Activities), included outings where we explored underwater environments.
